KEY MESSAGE 1...Strong storm system is expected to bring strong
easterly winds, heavy rain, coastal/tidal flooding and 
dangerous marine conditions Thanksgiving afternoon into early on
Friday. 

Strong, well-developed low pressure is still expected to impact 
Southern New England starting around the afternoon of Thanksgiving 
Day and continue into early on Friday. This period is where the 
greatest number of anticipated adverse impacts are expected, 
although lesser but residual effects are expected to linger into 
Friday. As the Key Message above states, there are plenty of hazards 
to contend with, so we'll talk about each in detail below...

Rain: The presence of an antecedent 1043 mb high pressure over 
northern New England will supply enough dry air to keep an advancing 
precipitation shield from reaching our southern coastal waters until 
around mid-morning on Thanksgiving Day, then spreading northward by 
around early-afternoon and towards the MA/VT/NH border area closer 
to mid- to late-afternoon on Thanksgiving. This timing should 
mitigate any risk for high-terrain frozen precip as sfc temps should 
have warmed up enough above freezing by the time precip begins, thus 
expecting all-rain throughout. Rain is expected to become steady, 
windswept and at-times heavy as we move into Thanksgiving evening 
into overnight. Although we don't expect this to be a widespread, 
significant flood event, rainfall could be enough to produce 
nuisance street and poor drainage flooding from leaf-clogged storm 
drains, and there are a few rivers in RI and eastern MA which HEFS-
based river stage guidance could approach or exceed bankfull stages 
(e.g. Wood River at Hope Valley, Pawtuxet River at Cranston, Taunton 
River at Bridgewater, Shawsheen River at Wilmington, and the North 
Nashua River at Fitchburg). Will need to monitor these rivers for 
rises and possible river flood warnings; however by early Friday 
morning, a dryslot races ENE and turns steady, heavy rain over to 
more of a lighter, showery character as we move into Black Friday as 
we get under the upper low and occluding/filling primary cyclone 
moving in from the northern mid-Atlantic states. So the bulk of the 
rain really falls during the Thanksgiving afternoon to the pre-dawn 
Friday hours. Total rainfall ranges from 1.5-2.5" across eastern and 
central MA and much of RI, with a second maxima around the 
Berkshires of 1-1.5" due to upslope enhancement, with some precip 
shadowing in the CT valley supporting rain totals here of around an 
inch. 

Strong Winds: There remains a robust signal for strong easterly 
winds to affect Southern New England, peaking Thanksgiving early-
evening into the overnight hours, coincident with the period of 
heaviest rain. The GFS still remains the most robust, showing 
easterly 950 mb winds between 45-65 kt for the eastern roughly half 
of Southern New England, greatest in southeast New England. The Wind 
Advisory was maintained for much of coastal New England; however we 
also added Wind Advisories for the higher terrain in Worcester, 
Tolland and Windham Counties as well as the east slopes of the 
Berkshires from noon Thanksgiving Day through early Friday morning. 
It's really more of a downslope component to the wind and we don't 
commonly see strong downslope winds, but with the GFS and HRRR 
showing ridgetop-winds around 45-50 kt, we felt it was borderline 
but close enough to consider wind headlines. Wind gusts of up to 50 
mph are expected, but could punch upwards of 55 mph over coastal
Southern New England. Tree and powerline damage could be 
possible, with the best potential in the Wind Advisory areas. 

Marine: Dangerous marine conditions are expected due to strong 
easterly winds and building rough seas Thursday mid-morning into 
overnight. See the Marine section for more details.

Tidal/Coastal Flooding: Tides are at their astronomically-highest 
over the next couple of days, which elevates the risk for coastal 
flooding, with the high tides being the highest during the daytime 
hours. The two high tides of most concern are the Thursday mid-
evening high tide for the RI/MA south coast, and the Friday early 
afternoon high tide for eastern MA. Latest storm surge guidance 
suggests around a 1.5-2 ft storm surge with the strongest easterly 
winds, taking place during the evening and overnight. Given this 
timing, this slots the peak surge within the lower of the two high 
tides for the RI/MA south coast, and during or just after the 
overnight/pre-dawn low tide period for the eastern MA coast. Since 
there should be some additional wave action/setup given the nearly 
20 ft waves offshore, we opted to issue coastal flood advisories 
covering both the south coast and the eastern coasts. In fact for 
the eastern MA coast, the time of high tide should coincide with a 
decrease in storm surge. Around one-half to one foot of inundation 
is anticipated, mainly for the typically vulnerable coastal and 
shoreline
